title: Linear Momentum and Impulse
notes: **Linear momentum:** $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$. It is a vector quantity pointing in the same direction as velocity. Momentum measures the "quantity of motion" an object possesses and is fundamental to analyzing collisions and interactions.

**Impulse:** $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}\,dt \approx \vec{F}_{avg}\Delta t$. Impulse equals the product of the average force and the time interval over which it acts. For a constant force, $\vec{J} = \vec{F}\Delta t$. Impulse has the same units as momentum: $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ or $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$.

**Impulse-Momentum Theorem:** $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$. This follows directly from Newton's second law: $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$, so $\int\vec{F}\,dt = \Delta\vec{p}$. This theorem is often more useful than $F = ma$ when forces act over short time intervals.

**Why impulse matters in safety:** a large force acting for a short time can produce the same momentum change as a smaller force acting for a longer time. This is why airbags and crumple zones work — they increase the impact time, reducing the average force on passengers. A collision lasting 0.01 s exerts 10 times the force of one lasting 0.1 s for the same momentum change.

**Units:** momentum has units of $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ or equivalently $\text{N}\cdot\text{s}$. These are dimensionally identical: $[M][L][T]^{-1} = [M][L][T]^{-2} \times [T]$. Always use SI units consistently when solving problems.
**Dimensional analysis:** $[p] = [M][L][T]^{-1}$, $[J] = [M][L][T]^{-1}$. Both have the same dimensions, confirming $J = \Delta p$. Dimensional consistency is a powerful check on derived formulas.

**Relation to kinetic energy:** while $p = mv$, kinetic energy is $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$. Two objects with the same momentum but different masses have different kinetic energies — the lighter object has more kinetic energy. This is why a bullet (small mass, high speed) carries more energy than a slow-moving truck with the same momentum.

**Momentum vs. energy:** momentum is a vector and conserved in all isolated systems; kinetic energy is a scalar and only conserved in elastic collisions. Both are essential tools for analyzing collisions.

**Relativistic momentum:** at speeds comparable to light, $\vec{p} = \gamma m\vec{v}$ where $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}$. The impulse-momentum theorem still holds, but the classical expression $p = mv$ underestimates momentum at high speeds. For NEB exams, use classical formulas only unless relativity is specified.

**Rocket propulsion:** a rocket accelerates by expelling gas at high speed. The thrust force is $F = v_e \frac{dm}{dt}$, where $v_e$ is the exhaust velocity. This is an application of the impulse-momentum principle to a system of variable mass. The famous rocket equation is $v_f = v_e \ln\frac{m_0}{m_f}$.

**Collisions and impulse:** during a collision, the impulse delivered to each object equals the average force times the contact time. Even though forces are enormous and brief, the impulse is finite and equals the change in momentum of each object.

**Graphical interpretation:** the impulse equals the area under a force-time graph. For a non-constant force, you must integrate. A rectangular approximation using average force is valid when the force profile is roughly constant.

**Impulse in sports:** a golfer's drive involves an impulse of about 4 N·s delivered in 0.001 s, producing an average force of 4000 N. A cricket batsman "follows through" to increase contact time and thus impulse, sending the ball farther.

**Momentum of a system:** the total momentum of a system of particles is $\vec{p}_{total} = \sum_i m_i\vec{v}_i = M\vec{v}_{cm}$, where $M$ is the total mass and $\vec{v}_{cm}$ is the velocity of the center of mass.

**Newton's second law in momentum form:** $\vec{F} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$ is the original formulation by Newton and is more general than $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$. It applies to systems with changing mass (rockets) and is the foundation of conservation laws.

**Stopping distance and impulse:** for a vehicle braking to rest, the impulse equals the initial momentum: $J = mv_0$. The stopping force depends on how quickly the vehicle stops: $F_{avg} = \frac{mv_0}{\Delta t}$. Doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy but doubles the impulse.

**Impulse and pressure waves:** in acoustics, a sound pulse delivers a tiny impulse to the eardrum. The impulse-momentum theorem explains how sound waves transfer energy and momentum through a medium.

**Units check:** $[p] = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s} = [M][L][T]^{-1}$ and $[J] = \text{N}\cdot\text{s} = [M][L][T]^{-2}\cdot[T] = [M][L][T]^{-1}$. The dimensional equality confirms the impulse-momentum relationship.
confusion: Momentum and kinetic energy are often confused because both involve mass and velocity. Key difference: momentum is a vector ($\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$) while kinetic energy is a scalar ($K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$). Two objects with the same momentum can have very different kinetic energies.

Impulse is NOT the same as work. Work is $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$ (force times displacement); impulse is $\vec{J} = \vec{F} \Delta t$ (force times time). They have different physical meanings and are measured by different instruments.

A force acting perpendicular to the motion changes the direction of momentum but not its magnitude — this is uniform circular motion. Impulse still occurs, but it changes the momentum vector's direction, not its length.
In a collision, impulse is equal and opposite on the two colliding objects (Newton's third law), but the momentum change of each object depends on its mass and the duration of the force.

The term "momentum" in everyday language ("the team has momentum") is not the same as physical momentum. In physics, momentum is precisely defined as $m\vec{v}$ and is always conserved in an isolated system.

Impulse depends on the time duration of the force, not just its magnitude. A small force acting for a long time can produce the same impulse as a large force acting briefly. This is why padded surfaces reduce injury — they extend the impact time.

Momentum is conserved in the direction where no external force acts, even if momentum is not conserved in other directions. For example, a projectile in flight conserves horizontal momentum but not vertical momentum (gravity acts downward).

The impulse-momentum theorem applies to both constant and variable forces. For variable forces, you must integrate: $\vec{J} = \int \vec{F}(t)\,dt$. The average force formulation $\vec{J} = \vec{F}_{avg}\Delta t$ is a shorthand for this integral.
practice: A 0.15 kg baseball moving at 40 m/s is hit by a bat and returns at 50 m/s in the opposite direction. If the contact time is 0.002 s, find the average force exerted by the bat. Solution: Taking the initial direction as positive: $p_i = 0.15 \times 40 = 6$ kg·m/s, $p_f = 0.15 \times (-50) = -7.5$ kg·m/s. $\Delta p = -7.5 - 6 = -13.5$ kg·m/s. $F_{avg} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{-13.5}{0.002} = -6750$ N. The average force is 6750 N opposite to the initial direction.

A 2000 kg car travelling at 20 m/s comes to rest in 5 seconds. Find the impulse and the average braking force. Solution: $J = \Delta p = 0 - (2000 \times 20) = -40000$ N·s. $F_{avg} = \frac{J}{\Delta t} = \frac{-40000}{5} = -8000$ N. The negative sign indicates the force opposes the motion.

A 10 g bullet moving at 500 m/s strikes a stationary 2 kg block on a frictionless surface and embeds itself. Find the final velocity of the block-bullet system. Solution: Conservation of momentum: $m_b v_b = (m_b + m_{block})v_f$. $0.01 \times 500 = (0.01 + 2) v_f$, so $v_f = \frac{5}{2.01} \approx 2.49$ m/s.

A tennis ball of mass 0.06 kg is served at 30 m/s. If the racket is in contact with the ball for 0.005 s, what is the average force? Solution: $J = \Delta p = 0.06 \times 30 - 0 = 1.8$ N·s. $F_{avg} = \frac{1.8}{0.005} = 360$ N.

Explain why a goalkeeper pulls his hands backward when catching a fast ball. Solution: By pulling his hands backward, the goalkeeper increases the time over which the ball's momentum is brought to zero. Since $F_{avg} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, a larger $\Delta t$ means a smaller average force on the hands, reducing the chance of injury.

A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s hits a wall and rebounds at 6 m/s in the opposite direction. If the contact time is 0.02 s, find the average force exerted by the wall. Solution: Taking the initial direction as positive: $p_i = 0.5 \times 8 = 4$ kg·m/s, $p_f = 0.5 \times (-6) = -3$ kg·m/s. $\Delta p = -3 - 4 = -7$ kg·m/s. $F_{avg} = \frac{-7}{0.02} = -350$ N. The wall exerts 350 N on the ball.

A raindrop of mass 0.003 kg falls vertically at 10 m/s and hits the ground, coming to rest in 0.001 s. Find the average force exerted by the ground on the drop. Solution: $\Delta p = 0 - (0.003 \times 10) = -0.03$ N·s. $F_{avg} = \frac{-0.03}{0.001} = -30$ N. The ground exerts 30 N upward on the drop.

A 50 g ball moving at 20 m/s is caught by a player. If the player's hands move back 0.3 m during the catch, find the average force and the time of contact. Solution: Using work-energy: the impulse equals the change in momentum, $J = 0.05 \times 20 = 1$ N·s. If the hands move 0.3 m while decelerating uniformly, the average speed during contact is 10 m/s, so $\Delta t = \frac{0.3}{10} = 0.03$ s. $F_{avg} = \frac{1}{0.03} = 33.3$ N.
universalFacts: The impulse-momentum theorem is another way of stating Newton's second law, but it is often more useful than $F = ma$ when forces vary with time or act over short intervals.
In space, a small thruster firing for a long time can produce the same momentum change as a large thruster firing briefly — this is the principle behind ion propulsion systems.
The SI unit of momentum, kg·m/s, is equivalent to the N·s (newton-second), the unit of impulse. This equivalence reflects the impulse-momentum theorem.
In particle physics, momentum is conserved in all interactions, including those where kinetic energy is not conserved (e.g., inelastic collisions at the subatomic level).
A heavy truck at low speed can have the same momentum as a light bullet at high speed — for example, a 3000 kg truck at 2 m/s has $p = 6000$ kg·m/s, the same as a 0.01 kg bullet at 600 m/s.

The concept of impulse explains why eggs don't break when caught with soft hands but do break when caught with stiff hands. Soft hands increase contact time, reducing the average force for the same impulse.
In automotive safety engineering, the crumple zone is designed to increase the collision time from about 0.05 s to 0.15 s, reducing the peak force on passengers by a factor of approximately 3.

The momentum of light is given by $p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant and $\lambda$ is the wavelength. This is the basis for solar sail propulsion in space exploration.
